title: The preachers, women and men
hook: he sends out preachers to lead sangats, women among them, and speaks against the burning of widows

segments.voice: Yesterday: pangat, the row, and an emperor on the floor at Goindval. Nobody sits at the head.

When something starts to grow, a small business, a club, a movement, there comes a moment when the founder can't be everywhere. People are joining in towns far away. They want to learn, and they can't all travel to one village by the river. That's where the Sikhs were by the time of Guru Amar Das, with communities across the Punjab and beyond. So the Guru did something practical. He chose trusted people and sent them out, each to look after a region, teach the hymns and gather the community. And tradition says some of those he trusted with this were women.
screen: `THE FOUNDER CAN'T BE EVERYWHERE.` → `COMMUNITIES ACROSS THE PUNJAB.` → `TRUSTED TEACHERS, SENT OUT.`

segments.voice: The word is manji. A manji is a simple cot, a low wooden frame strung with rope, the kind people sat on in Punjabi courtyards. The teacher sat on the manji, and the community gathered on the ground around it. So manji came to mean the teaching post itself: the seat, and the responsibility that went with it. Sikh tradition speaks of twenty-two manjis set up by Guru Amar Das, spreading the teaching across a wide region. And tradition says women were among those trusted to teach and lead. The Guru also spoke directly about women's lives. One practice of that time and place was sati, the burning of a widow on her husband's funeral fire. In a hymn in the scripture, Guru Amar Das redefines the word. A true sati, he says, is not a woman who burns herself on her husband's pyre; it's one who lives with goodness and contentment, and honors her beloved by how she lives. He's also remembered for discouraging the veil for women at the gathering, and for standing against the idea that a woman's worth ended with her husband's life. Behind it all is a line of Guru Nanak's that Sikhs quote often. Why call her lesser, he asks, from whom kings are born? We are born of woman, we are married to woman, it is through woman that the world goes on. To be honest, Sikh communities, like others, have lived up to this unevenly. But the Gurus' words are clear, and they're in the book.
screen: `MANJI — A COT, THEN A TEACHING SEAT.` · `TWENTY-TWO MANJIS, TRADITION SAYS.` · `A TRUE SATI LIVES, IN GOODNESS.` · `WHY CALL HER LESSER?` · then, large: `SHE IS NOT LESSER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one woman who taught you: a mother or grandmother, a teacher, a boss, an older sister, a neighbor, a friend, someone who sat, in a way, on a manji for you. Remember one thing she taught you, in words or without them. If she's alive, think how you'd tell her; if she's gone, just thank her, quietly.
Manji. A simple rope cot, and the teaching seat Guru Amar Das gave trusted women and men to lead communities. Today's word.
Your line: she is not lesser. Tomorrow, the song of bliss. That's day fifty-two, well spent.

howItsDone: In Sikh practice any person, woman or man, may lead prayer, read from the Guru Granth Sahib or perform kirtan; Sikhs cite Guru Nanak's words on women and Guru Amar Das's teaching on sati as part of the Gurus' stand for women's equality.

original.note: Gurmukhi: manji, a low rope-strung cot; the teacher sat on it, and the name came to mean the teaching post.

trapdoor: what you thought: a piece of furniture.
what it means: a seat of teaching and trust, given to women and men, in a time when women's worth was often denied.
what a scholar hears: the manji system of twenty-two regional posts; Guru Amar Das's Var Suhi, around Ang 787, on sati; and Guru Nanak's Asa di Var, Ang 473, on women.

chat.says: What did Guru Amar Das teach about women?
options: He trusted women to lead, and redefined sati: a true sati lives with goodness.
He sent preachers out, but tradition says every one of them was a man.
He kept every old custom, and made the veil a rule at the gathering.
chat.meaning: Tradition says women were among those given manjis. He redefined sati, and Sikhs quote Nanak: why call her lesser, from whom kings are born?

notes: Twenty-two manjis: common tradition; whether women held manjis (or the separate 'piris' sometimes mentioned, e.g. 52 piris) needs a historian's check. The script says 'tradition says women were among those trusted to teach and lead'. Confirm.
Sati salok at Ang 787 (satiaa eh na aakheeani...), paraphrased. Confirm Ang and paraphrase.
Asa di Var salok 'so kio mandaa aakheeai jit jameh raajaan', Ang 473, paraphrased. Confirm.
Guru Amar Das discouraging the veil (the Rani of Haripur story) stated as 'remembered for'; confirm.
Candid line on communities living up to this 'unevenly'; a Keeper should confirm tone.
